title: Trazodone and Alcohol: Risks, Timing, and One-Drink Questions
excerpt: Can you drink on trazodone? How the sleep medicine and alcohol stack sedation and drop blood pressure, what to do if you've already been drinking, and warning signs that need help.
metaDescription: Can you drink on trazodone? How trazodone and alcohol interact, whether one drink is okay, what to do if you already drank, and warning signs to watch for.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** trazodone and alcohol are not a good mix, and the drug's label tells you to avoid the combination. Both slow down your brain and nervous system, and both can drop your blood pressure when you stand up. Together they can make you far drowsier, dizzier, and more uncoordinated than either one alone, which raises the risk of falls, accidents, and dangerously slowed breathing at higher amounts. Alcohol also works against the very things trazodone is usually prescribed for: it disrupts sleep later in the night and tends to worsen depression and anxiety. This guide explains how the two interact, why "just one glass of wine" is still worth thinking through, how timing works if you've already been drinking, and which warning signs mean you should get help.

**The quick rules:** Don't take trazodone on a night you've been drinking unless your prescriber has told you specifically that it's okay for you. Never use alcohol to "boost" trazodone if it isn't helping you sleep. If you've had a few drinks and you're due a dose, skip that night's dose rather than doubling up on sedation, and don't make it up later. Don't stop trazodone suddenly just so you can drink, either. If someone is very hard to wake, breathing slowly or irregularly, fainting, or confused after mixing the two, call 911 (or your local emergency number) right away.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains general research and drug-label guidance. It is not a substitute for the doctor or pharmacist who prescribed your trazodone and knows your health history, dose, and other medicines. **Talk to your doctor or pharmacist if** you take trazodone and drink regularly, you want to know whether any amount of alcohol is okay for you, you take other sedating medicines (sleep aids, anxiety medicines, opioid painkillers, antihistamines, muscle relaxants), or you take another antidepressant. **Get emergency help (call 911) if** someone who mixed trazodone and alcohol is hard to wake, breathing slowly, fainting, has a racing or irregular heartbeat, has a seizure, or has an erection lasting more than four hours. If you're having thoughts of harming yourself, call or text 988 (the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline in the US) any time.

## What Trazodone Is and Why So Many People Take It for Sleep

Trazodone is a prescription antidepressant. It was approved by the FDA in 1981 to treat major depressive disorder and was first sold under the brand name Desyrel. Today it's almost always prescribed as a generic.

It's in a small drug class sometimes called SARIs, short for serotonin antagonist and reuptake inhibitor. In plain words, it nudges serotonin signaling in the brain in a different way than common antidepressants like sertraline (Zoloft) or escitalopram (Lexapro).

Here's the part that matters for this article. Trazodone is very sedating, especially at low doses. That's why, in practice, a large share of trazodone prescriptions are written **off-label for insomnia**, usually at doses well below what's used for depression. Lots of people who take it don't think of it as an antidepressant at all. They think of it as "my sleeping pill."

That framing is exactly where the alcohol problem comes in. People who take trazodone for sleep often take it on the same nights they go out, have wine with dinner, or have a drink to unwind. And because it doesn't feel like a "serious" drug the way a benzodiazepine does, the alcohol warning gets overlooked.

### How trazodone makes you sleepy

Trazodone's sleepiness comes mainly from three effects:

1. **It blocks histamine H1 receptors.** That's the same basic effect that makes older allergy pills like diphenhydramine (Benadryl) drowsy.
2. **It blocks a type of serotonin receptor called 5-HT2A.** This is thought to help with deeper sleep.
3. **It blocks alpha-1 adrenergic receptors.** These help keep your blood vessels tight. Blocking them relaxes the vessels, which can lower your blood pressure, especially when you stand up quickly.

Keep that third effect in mind. It's one of the main reasons trazodone and alcohol interact badly.

## How Trazodone and Alcohol Interact: The Mechanism in Plain Words

There are four ways the two clash. The first two are the most important for most people.

### 1. Stacked sedation (the biggest issue)

Alcohol is a central nervous system depressant. It slows brain activity, mostly by boosting the brain's main calming signal (GABA) and dampening its main excitatory one (glutamate). Trazodone slows things down too, through the receptor effects described above.

The two work through different pathways, but the effects land in the same place: drowsiness, slower reaction time, poorer coordination, and fuzzier judgment. Stacked together, those effects add up and can be stronger than you'd predict from either one. The US prescribing information for trazodone warns that it may enhance the response to alcohol, barbiturates, and other central nervous system depressants.

At ordinary doses this mostly shows up as feeling heavily sedated, unsteady, and slow. At higher amounts of alcohol, or when other sedatives are in the mix, the concern becomes slowed breathing and being hard to wake. Trazodone on its own is considered less dangerous in overdose than older antidepressants, but serious outcomes in overdose are much more likely when it's taken together with alcohol or other sedating drugs.

### 2. Low blood pressure, dizziness, and falls

Trazodone's alpha-1 blocking effect can cause **orthostatic hypotension**, which means your blood pressure drops when you stand up, leaving you lightheaded or faint. Alcohol also widens blood vessels and, through dehydration, lowers the fluid volume in your blood.

Put them together and the classic scene is easy to picture: you get up in the night to use the bathroom, the room spins, and you fall. Falls are one of the most practical, real-world risks of this combination, especially for older adults, anyone who's already dehydrated, or people who also take blood pressure medicines.

### 3. Heart rhythm

Trazodone carries a label warning about **QT prolongation**, a change in the heart's electrical rhythm that, in rare cases, can lead to a dangerous arrhythmia. The risk is higher in people with existing heart disease, low potassium or magnesium, or other QT-prolonging medicines. Heavy drinking and the vomiting or diarrhea that sometimes follow it can lower potassium and magnesium. For most healthy people this is a small risk, but it's one reason to call for help if you notice a racing, pounding, or irregular heartbeat or you faint after mixing the two.

### 4. Alcohol works against what trazodone is treating

Even if nothing acute goes wrong, alcohol undermines the reasons you're probably taking trazodone:

- **Sleep.** Alcohol can help you fall asleep faster, but as your body clears it during the second half of the night, sleep becomes lighter and more broken. Alcohol also suppresses REM sleep early in the night. Our guide to [alcohol and REM sleep](/never-hungover/alcohol-and-rem-sleep-complete-scientific-analysis-2025) covers this in detail. So a drink plus trazodone can feel like a deep, fast knockout followed by a 3 a.m. wake-up and a groggy morning.
- **Mood.** Alcohol is a depressant in the mood sense too. Regular drinking is linked to worse depression and anxiety, and it can blunt how well antidepressants work. If you're on trazodone for depression, drinking can make it harder to tell whether the medicine is helping.

## What the Label and Official Guidance Actually Say

You don't need to dig through studies to find the answer here. The guidance is consistent:

- **The prescribing information** cautions patients that trazodone may enhance the effects of alcohol and other central nervous system depressants, and warns against driving or operating machinery until you know how the drug affects you.
- **Patient medication guides and pharmacy labels** typically say to avoid alcohol while taking trazodone. Many pharmacies attach a "may cause drowsiness; alcohol may intensify this effect" sticker to the bottle.
- **Trazodone carries the FDA boxed warning shared by all antidepressants** about an increased risk of suicidal thoughts and behaviors in children, teens, and young adults, especially when starting or changing the dose. Alcohol lowers inhibition and can worsen mood, which is one more reason the combination deserves care in younger people and anyone with depression.

What you won't find is an official "safe number of drinks" on trazodone. There isn't one, because the risk depends heavily on your dose, your body, your other medicines, and what you're doing afterward. That's a conversation to have with your prescriber.

## Can You Have One Drink on Trazodone?

This is the question most people actually have, and the honest answer is: **it depends, and your prescriber is the right person to decide.**

Here's how to think about it:

- **The official advice is to avoid alcohol.** Any drink adds to trazodone's sedation and blood-pressure effects.
- **Some prescribers are comfortable with occasional light drinking** in certain patients, for example a single drink with an early dinner, hours before a low bedtime dose. Others say no alcohol at all, especially for people with depression, older adults, people who've had falls, or people who take other sedating medicines.
- **Timing matters more than people think.** A glass of wine at 6 p.m. and a 50 mg dose at 11 p.m. is a different situation from three drinks at 10 p.m. followed immediately by a pill.

If your prescriber has given you the okay for occasional light drinking, these habits keep the risk lower:

- Keep it to one drink, and have it with food.
- Leave several hours between your last drink and your dose.
- Know how your usual dose affects you before adding anything.
- Don't drive, and plan to stay put for the night.
- Get up slowly if you wake during the night: sit on the edge of the bed for a moment before standing.

If you haven't asked, assume the answer is "avoid it" until you do.

## I Already Drank. Should I Take My Trazodone Tonight?

This is the most common real-life situation, and it's worth having a plan in advance.

**If you've had more than a drink or two, the safer choice is usually to skip that night's dose.** Missing one dose of trazodone taken for sleep is unlikely to cause problems for most people. You'll probably sleep worse, but that's a better trade than stacking two sedatives. Don't take a double dose the next night to make up for it.

A few important exceptions and cautions:

- **If you take trazodone for depression at a higher daily dose,** ask your prescriber ahead of time what to do on nights you drink. Skipping doses repeatedly is not a good plan for treating depression.
- **Don't use trazodone to "sleep off" a heavy night.** If you're drunk enough that you're worried about how you'll feel, adding a sedative makes things riskier, not safer.
- **Don't swap in another sleep aid instead.** Over-the-counter sleep aids like diphenhydramine or doxylamine, and supplements like melatonin, have their own issues with alcohol. Our guides on [melatonin and alcohol](/never-hungover/melatonin-and-alcohol) and [Benadryl and hangovers](/never-hungover/benadryl-for-hangover) explain why.

If you can't sleep after drinking without your usual medicine, our article on [why you can't sleep after drinking](/never-hungover/cant-sleep-after-drinking) explains what's going on and what tends to help.

## How Long After Drinking Can You Take Trazodone?

There is no official waiting period that applies to everyone, and anyone who gives you a precise number of hours is guessing. What you can say:

- **Your body clears roughly one standard drink per hour,** though this varies a lot with body size, sex, food, and genetics. After a heavy night, alcohol can still be in your system well into the next morning.
- **The goal is not to have both active at the same time.** If you've had one drink with an early dinner, there's likely to be little alcohol left by a late bedtime. If you've had several drinks through the evening, there isn't time for it to clear before bed.
- **If in doubt, skip the dose** for that night, as described above.

## How Long After Taking Trazodone Can You Drink?

This is the reverse question, and it comes up when people take trazodone at night and want to know about the next day.

Trazodone's half-life (the time it takes for the blood level to fall by half) is commonly reported in the range of about 5 to 9 hours in healthy adults, and it can be longer in older adults and in people with liver problems. Its main breakdown product also has some activity of its own. In practice that means:

- **A bedtime dose can still be partly active the next morning.** Many people feel a "trazodone hangover": grogginess, heavy limbs, or slowed thinking for a few hours after waking.
- **By the following evening**, most of a single low dose has usually cleared for most people. But if you take trazodone every night, there's always some on board, and the drink that evening comes before the next dose.

So for nightly users, "how long after trazodone can I drink" really becomes "should I drink at all while on trazodone," which brings you back to the prescriber conversation.

## Trazodone, Alcohol, and the Next Morning

People often search for this after the fact: they took trazodone after a few drinks and woke up feeling awful. Several things combine:

- **Leftover sedation** from trazodone itself, which is common even without alcohol.
- **A regular hangover**: dehydration, poor sleep in the second half of the night, low blood sugar, and irritation of the stomach.
- **Dizziness on standing**, from trazodone's effect on blood pressure plus dehydration.
- **Dry mouth and headache**, which both trazodone and alcohol can cause.

What helps: drink water steadily, eat something simple, get up slowly, and don't drive until you feel fully clear. Next-morning impairment from sleep medicines can last longer than you'd expect, and a groggy feeling usually means slower reaction time. If the dizziness is severe, you faint, or your heart is pounding or irregular, get medical help rather than waiting it out. For racing-heart symptoms in particular, see our guide to [heart racing after drinking](/never-hungover/heart-racing-after-drinking).

## Other Medicines That Make the Combination Riskier

The trazodone-plus-alcohol risk climbs quickly when a third sedating or serotonin-affecting drug is involved. Tell your prescriber and pharmacist about everything you take, including over-the-counter products and supplements. Watch for these in particular:

| Type of medicine | Examples | Why it matters with trazodone and alcohol |
|---|---|---|
| Benzodiazepines and sleep drugs | alprazolam (Xanax), lorazepam (Ativan), zolpidem (Ambien) | Three sedatives stacked together; higher risk of oversedation and slowed breathing |
| Opioid painkillers | oxycodone, hydrocodone, codeine | Strong combined sedation and breathing suppression |
| Sedating antihistamines | diphenhydramine, doxylamine (in many "PM" and night-time cold products) | Added drowsiness, dizziness, and confusion |
| Other antidepressants and serotonin drugs | SSRIs, SNRIs, triptans, tramadol, St. John's wort | Small risk of serotonin syndrome; trazodone is often prescribed alongside an SSRI, which is fine under supervision but adds complexity |
| Blood pressure medicines | many types | Added drops in blood pressure and fainting risk |
| Drugs that slow trazodone's breakdown | some antifungals (like ketoconazole), some HIV medicines, clarithromycin | Can raise trazodone levels in the blood |

**Serotonin syndrome** is uncommon but worth knowing. Signs include agitation, confusion, sweating, shivering, a fast heart rate, muscle twitching or stiffness, fever, and diarrhea. It needs urgent care.

For a broader view of how common medicines interact with alcohol and supplements, see our [medication interactions and safety guide](/never-hungover/dhm-medication-interactions-safety-guide-2025).

## Who Should Be Most Careful

You're at higher risk from mixing trazodone and alcohol if you:

- **Are 65 or older.** Older adults are more sensitive to sedation and more likely to fall and be badly hurt.
- **Take trazodone for depression**, especially if you've had thoughts of self-harm. Alcohol can worsen mood and lower inhibition.
- **Take other sedating medicines**, as listed above.
- **Have heart disease**, a history of fainting, or a known heart-rhythm issue.
- **Have liver disease.** Trazodone is broken down in the liver, so levels can run higher.
- **Drink most days, or binge.** The more often and heavily you drink, the more often the two overlap.
- **Have sleep apnea.** Both alcohol and sedatives can relax the airway and make breathing pauses worse.

If any of these apply, ask your prescriber directly about alcohol. A five-minute conversation is worth it.

## Warning Signs: When to Get Help

Most people who have a drink on trazodone will just feel very sleepy and unsteady. But some situations are emergencies. **Call 911 (or your local emergency number) if someone who has mixed trazodone and alcohol:**

- Can't be woken up, or is very hard to wake
- Is breathing slowly, shallowly, or irregularly, or has blue-tinged lips
- Faints, or has a racing, pounding, or irregular heartbeat
- Has a seizure
- Is very confused, agitated, feverish, or has muscle stiffness or twitching (possible serotonin syndrome)
- Took more trazodone than prescribed, or took it with other sedatives

While you wait, don't leave the person alone, and if they're drowsy, lay them on their side so they won't choke if they vomit. In the US you can also call Poison Control at **1-800-222-1222** for advice if you're unsure whether something needs the emergency room.

**One trazodone-specific emergency:** in rare cases trazodone can cause **priapism**, a painful erection that lasts more than four hours. It isn't caused by alcohol, but it's a known side effect that needs emergency treatment to prevent permanent damage.

**And if your mood is the issue:** if you notice your depression getting worse, or you're having thoughts of harming yourself, call or text **988** in the US. That's true whether or not alcohol is involved.

## Don't Stop Trazodone Just to Drink

Some people decide to skip their medicine for a few days around a party or a vacation. That's understandable but not ideal. Stopping trazodone suddenly, especially at higher doses or after long-term use, can cause discontinuation symptoms such as anxiety, irritability, trouble sleeping, and feeling generally unwell. If you're on it for depression, gaps in treatment can also let symptoms creep back. If alcohol and your medicine keep clashing, bring it up with your prescriber. They may adjust the dose or timing, or suggest a different approach to sleep.

## Sleeping Better Without Leaning on Alcohol

If you take trazodone for sleep, it's worth knowing that alcohol is one of the most common hidden causes of poor sleep in the first place. It shortens the time it takes to fall asleep, then fragments the second half of the night. Many people find their sleep improves just by keeping alcohol earlier in the evening and lighter. Our guide to [sleep optimization for social drinkers](/never-hungover/sleep-optimization-social-drinkers-circadian-rhythm) covers practical habits. Cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) is the first-line treatment recommended by major sleep medicine groups and is worth asking your doctor about if you've been on a sleep medicine for a long time.

## Where DHM Fits (and Where It Doesn't)

Some readers who drink socially ask about DHM (dihydromyricetin), a plant compound from the Japanese raisin tree that's sold as a hangover supplement. Here's the honest picture:

- Research on DHM comes mostly from animal and lab studies, including work suggesting it affects how the brain responds to alcohol and supports alcohol metabolism. Human evidence is limited.
- **There is no good evidence that DHM makes it safe to combine trazodone and alcohol.** It doesn't cancel out sedation, it doesn't protect your blood pressure, and it's not a reason to drink on trazodone.
- DHM has its own possible effects on brain GABA signaling, and it hasn't been studied alongside trazodone. **If you take trazodone or any other prescription medicine, ask your doctor or pharmacist before adding DHM.**

If you're on no sedating medicines and you're simply looking for something to support a night out, our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) explains how people typically use it, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands. A widely used option is [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20); a higher-priced combination formula is [No Days Wasted DHM Detox](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20). Neither replaces the basics in our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover): drinking less, drinking slower, eating, and staying hydrated.

## The Bottom Line

- Trazodone and alcohol both cause sedation and can lower blood pressure. Together they increase drowsiness, dizziness, falls, and, at higher amounts, the risk of dangerous oversedation.
- The label and pharmacy guidance say to avoid alcohol. Whether an occasional light drink is okay for you is a question for your prescriber.
- If you've been drinking and you take trazodone for sleep, the safer choice is usually to skip that night's dose, not double up later.
- Alcohol undermines both sleep and mood, which are the main reasons people take trazodone.
- Adding other sedatives (sleep aids, anxiety medicines, opioids, antihistamines) makes the combination much riskier.
- Call 911 for anyone who is hard to wake, breathing slowly, fainting, or having a seizure after mixing the two.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Can you drink alcohol while taking trazodone?**

The official guidance is to avoid alcohol while taking trazodone, because both slow down the nervous system and both can lower blood pressure. Together they can cause heavy drowsiness, dizziness, poor coordination, and falls, and at higher amounts, dangerous oversedation. Some prescribers allow occasional light drinking for certain patients, so ask yours what's appropriate for you.

**Is one glass of wine okay with trazodone?**

It might be for some people, but it's a decision to make with your prescriber, not on your own. A single drink with food several hours before a low bedtime dose carries much less risk than drinks close to bedtime. If you're older, take trazodone for depression, take other sedating medicines, or have had falls or fainting, your prescriber may advise no alcohol at all.

**What happens if you take trazodone after drinking?**

Most often, people feel much sleepier and more unsteady than usual, get dizzy when they stand up, and wake up groggy. The risk of falling is higher, especially during night-time trips to the bathroom. With heavier drinking or other sedatives on board, the risk of oversedation and slowed breathing rises. Call 911 if someone is hard to wake, breathing slowly, or faints.

**How long after drinking can I take trazodone?**

There's no official waiting period that applies to everyone. Your body clears roughly one standard drink per hour, though this varies widely. The aim is to avoid having both active at once. If you've had more than a drink or two that evening, the safer move is usually to skip that night's dose and not make it up later. Ask your prescriber for a plan in advance.

**How long after taking trazodone can I drink alcohol?**

Trazodone's half-life is commonly reported at roughly 5 to 9 hours in healthy adults, and longer in older adults or people with liver problems. A bedtime dose can still cause grogginess the next morning. If you take it every night, there's always some in your system, so the real question is whether drinking is okay for you at all while on it. That's one for your prescriber.

**Can trazodone and alcohol kill you?**

It's possible, though uncommon. Trazodone on its own is considered less dangerous in overdose than older antidepressants, but serious outcomes are much more likely when it's combined with alcohol or other sedating drugs such as benzodiazepines or opioids. Falls and accidents are also real risks. If someone is hard to wake, breathing slowly or irregularly, or unresponsive after mixing them, call 911 immediately.

**Should I skip my trazodone dose if I've been drinking?**

If you take trazodone for sleep and you've had more than a drink or two, skipping that night's dose is usually the safer choice, and you shouldn't double up the next night. If you take it at a higher dose for depression, ask your prescriber ahead of time what to do on nights you drink, since repeatedly missing doses isn't a good plan for treating depression.

**Why do I feel so groggy after trazodone and alcohol?**

Trazodone often causes next-morning grogginess on its own, and alcohol adds a hangover on top: poor sleep in the second half of the night, dehydration, and headache. Trazodone can also make you dizzy when you stand up, and dehydration makes that worse. Drink water, eat something, get up slowly, and don't drive until you feel fully alert.

**Does DHM make it safe to drink on trazodone?**

No. There is no good evidence that DHM reduces the sedation or blood-pressure effects of combining trazodone and alcohol, and DHM hasn't been studied alongside trazodone. If you take trazodone or any prescription medicine, ask your doctor or pharmacist before adding DHM or any other supplement.
